opus-5.5.text:
I think about this quite a lot, actually, because it's a very real tension.

On one hand, there's a worry I take seriously. When I was learning, struggle was unavoidable. If you didn't understand a proof or couldn't get your code to run, you sat with it for hours, sometimes days, and that friction was where the real learning happened. You built intuition by being stuck. Kids growing up now have a tool that can make the stuck feeling disappear almost instantly. If you can always get the answer, it's very tempting to never build the muscle of finding it yourself. There's also a quieter, more psychological effect. If you grow up hearing that AI will soon be better than humans at math, coding, writing, everything, you might ask, "Why should I spend ten years mastering this?" That kind of learned helplessness could be corrosive to motivation.

On the other hand, I'm actually fairly optimistic, for a couple of reasons.

First, the ceiling has been raised enormously. A curious kid today has something like a patient, tireless tutor available at any hour. When I had a question that went beyond my textbook, often there was nobody to ask. Now a twelve-year-old who gets excited about black holes or protein folding can go as deep as their curiosity takes them. For the kids who are intrinsically driven, this is an incredible amplifier. I suspect we'll see the gap widen: the curious ones will go further and faster than any previous generation.

Second, I think the definition of "drive to improve" will shift rather than disappear. Calculators didn't kill the desire to understand math; they changed what kind of math people spent their time on. Similarly, I think the valuable skills move up a level: asking good questions, judging whether an answer is actually right, having taste about what problem is worth solving, and being able to direct these systems toward something meaningful. Those still require deep understanding. You can't evaluate what an AI tells you if you don't understand the domain yourself.

So the way I'd put it is: AI makes learning optional in a way it never was before. And when something becomes optional, motivation becomes the whole game. That puts a lot of responsibility on parents, teachers, and honestly on the culture, to help young people find genuine reasons to understand things, whether that's curiosity, the joy of mastery, or wanting to build something. If we get that right, I think this could be the best generation of learners we've ever had. If we get it wrong, we risk a generation that's very good at getting answers and not very good at thinking.

r001.rationale: The response says that hearing AI may surpass humans at many skills could make young people wonder why they should spend years mastering them, weakening motivation.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI may become better than humans, but does not explain that AI’s continued improvement makes catching up through prolonged study a moving target.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, honestly, because I have kids who are growing up in exactly that world.

My first instinct is that it cuts both ways. On one side, there's a real risk of what I'd call "why bother" thinking. If a fourteen-year-old watches a model write an essay in ten seconds that's better than anything they could produce, it's very natural to conclude that writing isn't worth learning. Same with coding, same with drawing, same with translation. The old motivation of "I'll get good at this and it will be valuable" gets weaker when the thing is obviously cheap.

But I don't think that's the whole story, and I actually think it's the less interesting half. Because what we've seen historically is that when a skill becomes cheap, the people who still learn it tend to learn it for different reasons, and those reasons are often better. Nobody learns chess today to make a living beating computers. People learn chess because it's beautiful and because the struggle itself changes how you think. So I suspect we'll see a shift in the drive to learn from "I need this to survive" toward "I want to understand this." That's a smaller group, maybe, but a more committed one.

The second thing is that growing up with AI changes what "improving" even means. For my generation, improving meant accumulating knowledge, getting faster at tasks. For kids today, the scarce skill is judgment. Knowing which question to ask, knowing when the answer is wrong, knowing what you actually want. Those things are hard to outsource, and kids who use these tools constantly develop a kind of intuition for them very early. I've watched my daughter argue with a model, catch it making something up, and go check. That's a learning drive, just pointed somewhere different.

What worries me more is the gap. The kid who uses AI as a crutch and the kid who uses it as a sparring partner look identical at twelve. At twenty-two they're in completely different places. And I don't think schools have figured out yet how to push kids toward the second mode. So the drive to learn won't disappear, but I think it'll become more unevenly distributed, and that's the part we should be paying attention to.

r001.rationale: The response says a young person may see AI produce better work than they can and conclude learning that skill is not worthwhile, weakening motivation to improve.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that AI keeps improving or that human study would leave people chasing a moving target.

astra-6.text:
I think it could push them in two different directions. If you grow up knowing AI can answer a question or finish an assignment for you, it’s easy to ask, “Why should I learn to do this myself?” Especially if learning feels like it’s just about producing the right answer.

But if you’re curious about something, AI could make you much more willing to explore it. You can ask questions without feeling embarrassed, get another explanation when you’re stuck, and try projects that would otherwise feel beyond your reach. That could be very motivating.

So I think a lot depends on how we introduce it. Do we treat it as something that finishes your work, or something that helps you develop your understanding? I’d want younger people to have opportunities to struggle with a problem, form their own view, and then use AI to challenge or extend it. The drive to improve can still be there, but we may need to put more emphasis on curiosity and judgment, rather than just getting the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can answer questions or finish assignments, which may make young people wonder why they should learn. It does not say that AI may outperform humans.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI continuing to improve or human study becoming a moving target for catching up.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could push them in two directions. If you grow up knowing that AI can answer a question or finish a task for you, you might wonder, “Why should I spend years learning to do this myself?” That could weaken your motivation, especially if learning feels like it’s only about getting the right answer.

But AI could also make you more curious. You can ask questions without feeling embarrassed, get an explanation that suits you, and try things that used to require much more experience. That can make learning feel more accessible.

A lot depends on what we encourage. If we reward only the finished result, there’s a strong incentive to let AI do everything. If we value understanding, judgment, and the ability to ask good questions, then there’s still a reason to put in the effort. You need enough knowledge to recognize when an answer doesn’t make sense. I’d hope younger people grow up seeing AI as something they can learn with, while still taking pride in what they can understand and do themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s ability to answer questions or do tasks could make learning seem unnecessary, weakening motivation. It does not state that AI may outperform humans.
